title: Bellvue Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Bellvue wells have a 348-foot median depth, with fractured-bedrock conditions affecting yield and drilling cost.
h1: Bellvue, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Bellvue means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well depths, and water production that can change from one parcel to the next. Records for permitted wells within 5 miles show a median depth of 348 feet, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 100 feet below the surface.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a specific lot. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so neighboring wells are among the best local evidence. Review the permit, construction, yield, and water-level records before you commit to a property.

sections.heading: Bellvue well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Bellvue wells are commonly drilled into fractured granite, gneiss, or other crystalline bedrock. The median recorded depth is 348 feet, while the middle half runs from 171 to 504 feet. That is a wide range for estimating a new well: a driller bidding only from the median may miss the conditions on your parcel.

The depth mix reinforces that variability. Thirty-nine percent of recorded wells are between 300 and 600 feet, 20% are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest record reaches 2,340 feet. Sixteen percent are under 100 feet, while 25% fall between 100 and 300 feet. For a bid, ask how the driller handles additional footage, casing, grout, and an unsuccessful hole.

sections.heading: What Bellvue wells produce
sections.html:
Among wells with reported pump yields, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 3.6 to 7.5 gallons per minute, and 68% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable range for ordinary household use, but a yield test and storage plan still matter.

Low-producing wells are a real part of the local record: 11% report less than 1 gallon per minute and 16% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A low-yield well may still serve a home if the pump, tank, and daily demand are designed around it. Confirm the permitted use; 95% of the records are domestic or household, with no irrigation wells shown in the use mix.

sections.heading: Bellvue water levels show no recorded decade shift
sections.html:
The median static water level is 100 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 54 to 200 feet. Static water level is measured when the well is not being pumped. It is not the same as the depth of the well, and it does not by itself tell you how much water the formation can deliver.

The available decade comparison shows a median of 100 feet below surface in the 2010s and 100 feet in the 2020s. That does not show a falling median water table in this dataset. The water-level sample is limited to 54 wells, so ask for the well-specific static level, pumping information, and any recent service records rather than relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Bellvue permit history and the drillers in the record
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across several decades. Records show 152 permits from the 1970s, 106 from the 1980s, 176 from the 1990s, 157 from the 2000s, 63 from the 2010s, and 49 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Older permits can still be valuable, but confirm that the recorded well location and construction details match the property.

The most active drillers in these records are High Desert Irrigation Llc (Hersh, Larry), with 162 wells; Hersh & Son Well Drilling Inc. (Hersh, Harry), with 152; and Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.), with 145. These records do not prove current availability or guarantee performance. A Colorado DWR permit and the final well construction report are the documents to compare.

sections.heading: Bellvue drilling cost starts with the rock
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock around Bellvue, the planning rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the recorded median depth of 348 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $22,600 to $34,800. That is the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $28,600 to $46,800 at that same median depth. A 504-foot well, near the top of the middle-half range, can materially exceed a median-depth allowance. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the hole must go deeper, produces less than expected, needs extra casing or grout, or is abandoned as a dry hole.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near Bellvue
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main physical risks in fractured bedrock. A strong neighboring well does not guarantee the same result because water depends on intersecting productive fractures. Have the seller provide the permit, construction report, pump information, water-quality tests, and service history. If the well is weak, confirm that storage and pumping equipment can support the intended household.

Environmental review also matters. Within about 10 miles, the mapped records include 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 23 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These locations do not automatically mean a property is contaminated. Test the actual well water and consider site-specific review. Septic setbacks, drainfield space, access for drilling equipment, and the home’s building location should be evaluated before closing.

sections.heading: A practical Bellvue plan for a lot or home
sections.html:
For an existing home, start with the well file and a current water test, then compare the reported yield with the home’s actual use. For vacant land, have a licensed driller review nearby permits before finalizing the homesite. Neighboring records around Bellvue, Laporte, Livermore, Drake, Glen Haven, Fort Collins, and Wellington can help show how conditions change across the broader area, but the closest comparable wells deserve the most weight.

Confirm the Colorado DWR permit and intended use before construction. Household-use wells have specific limits, including the general exempt-well pumping limit of 35 gallons per minute, and an augmentation plan may be required in an over-appropriated basin. Put drilling depth, testing, casing, grout, pump sizing, septic layout, and access in the project budget from the start.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Bellvue, Colorado?
faq.a: Bellvue wells have a median recorded depth of 348 feet. The middle half ranges from 171 to 504 feet, but 20% are 600 feet or deeper and the deepest record is 2,340 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes the actual depth highly parcel-specific, so nearby well permits are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Bellvue?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield near Bellvue is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.6 to 7.5 gallons per minute. Sixty-eight percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Still, 11% report less than 1 gallon per minute, so request the well’s yield test and plan storage around verified production.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Bellvue?
faq.a: The local fractured-bedrock planning rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 348-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $22,600 to $34,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $28,600 to $46,800. Extra depth, casing, grout, access, and a dry hole can change the final price.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Bellvue?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield. Test the actual well water, especially because mapped records within about 10 miles include 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 23 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific property, so use a qualified laboratory and review the results before buying.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Bellvue?
faq.a: The available records do not show a change in the median static water level: it is 100 feet below surface in both the 2010s and 2020s. The overall median is also 100 feet, with a middle half from 54 to 200 feet. Only 54 wells report static water levels, so check the specific well’s measurements rather than treating this as a guarantee.
